Bernstein puts the cost to the four largest airlines at about $345 million before tax; Bloomberg says airlines could lose more than $1 billion.

 SubjectiveThe Traveler — How the Nov. 13 FAA Ground Stop Shapes 2026 Holiday TravelA rare nationwide ground stop on November 13 has intensified scrutiny of the air traffic control network just as tens of millions of travellers head into the Thanksgiving and Christmas rush, with operations largely back to normal but political fallout and lingering disruption risks shaping how airlines and passengers plan the holidays. Federal statements attribute the disruption to problems within ageing network infrastructure interacting with ongoing modernisation work, not to a cyberattack. Early findings point to overloaded legacy switches and router hardware at several sites generating unusually high volumes of network traffic. Officials stress that these conclusions remain preliminary while contractors and federal investigators complete a technical root-cause analysis. Secretary Duffy and Administrator Bedford have both emphasised that there is currently no evidence of a malicious intrusion.

---

### Friday Closes With Wall Street in Correction After the Worst Week Since 2020, the Guardrails Given One Term in Washington, Nine Dead in Kyiv With the Alliance's Answer Still to Come, and a Tanker Still Unnamed in the Strait

Filed as: Edition No. 70 — The Midnight Watch · 2026-11-21T00:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-21-midnight-watch.html

The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Friday Closes With Wall Street in Correction After the Worst Week Since 2020, the Guardrails Given One Term in Washington, Nine Dead in Kyiv With the Alliance’s Answer Still to Come, and a Tanker Still Unnamed in the Strait

 The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a week closed in correction, with the chips down 17.1 percent; a guardrail that gained one term and no text; nine dead in Kyiv and three weapons down in Poland, unanswered by fire; a tanker burning off Khasab with no name in the file; a law passed in Paris and a verdict confirmed in Madrid; and a promised root cause that the week ends without.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Saturday, November 21, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 69, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Friday, in Edition No. 68, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Friday, in Edition No. 67, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Friday, and in Edition No. 66, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Friday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Friday Settled, What It Left Open

Friday settled the week’s measure, the guardrails’ one term, the French Senate’s vote, and Madrid’s verdict—and left the inquiry, the alliance’s answer, the tanker’s name, and the router’s verdict open at the turn of the log. Wall Street closed down 3.70 percent on the S&P 500 and 5.28 percent on the Nasdaq Composite, in the close account filed below, completing the worst week since March 2020 for two of the three indexes and a fall of 17.1 percent for the chip index, its worst week since 2001, in the weekly account filed below. Secretary Bessent said the guardrails agreed with President Xi carry one concrete term: a human being involved in every military decision the technology touches, in the Secretary’s account filed below. Kyiv’s count stands at nine dead, in the latest account filed below, and the weapons that fell in Poland were not fired on, in the assessment filed below. The tanker struck off Khasab stands unnamed in every account in the file. The desk takes the files in that order.

What Friday settled is the close and the week, the vote in Paris at 205 to 110, the debate’s verdict on two instruments, and the shape of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s inquiry as far as its reporting goes. What it left open is the rest: the guardrails’ text, the inquiry’s scope and the company’s answer, the Darnytskyi Bridge’s damage, the Security Council’s meeting, the strait’s weapon, and the root cause of the November 13 ground stop, promised for this week and not announced in it.

New York at Midnight: The Week’s Measure, Taken Whole

The evening file carried the close; the midnight file carries the week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points on Friday, or 1.93 percent, to 48,147.33, and 8.0 percent on the week, a drop of some 4,100 points and its worst week since March 2020; the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points, or 3.70 percent, to 6,910.39, and 8.6 percent on the week, its worst week since April 2025; and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1,261.47 points, or 5.28 percent, to 22,617.73, and 10.0 percent on the week, in the close account and the weekly account above. The Nasdaq 100 fell 10.4 percent on the week, its worst since March 2020, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 17.1 percent, its worst week since the week ending September 21, 2001, in the weekly account; the Russell 2000 fell 7.5 percent. The Dow and the S&P 500 closed in correction, down more than 10 percent from their peaks; the Nasdaq stands 18 percent below its October 6 record and negative for the year, its gain of 18.7 percent erased, in the year account filed below. The volatility index closed at 35.89, up 26.20 percent on the day and 86 percent on the week, in the pulse account filed below, having reached 38.50 in the week, its highest in 19 months, in the year account. The ten-year Treasury yield stood at 4.91 percent, down 14 basis points; Bitcoin at $58,955, down 4.76 percent, in the pulse account. Gold fell for a fifth straight day and 9 percent on the week, below $4,000 an ounce, and silver 15 percent, in the weekly wrap filed with the futures account below. Friday night’s only forward reading is a small one: the funds tracking the Dow, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 climbed 0.9, 1.0 and 1.5 percent in Friday-night trading, and the futures themselves reopen Sunday at 1800 Eastern, in the futures account filed below.

The debut’s second day ends five dollars above its price and no further. Anthropic closed at $88.30, down 9.1 percent, in the close account, and at $88.91, down 8.50 percent, in the quote account filed below—the desk prints the two closes in the Cocked Hat—after a low of $83.05, five cents above the $83 offering price, and an after-hours reading of $88.48 at 4:50 p.m. in the quote account. Thursday’s arc stands as the file printed it: priced at $83, first trade $111.50, high $115.10, close $97.17. The week’s question about the offering is now a question about Monday: whether the shares hold the price they were sold at when the market reopens after its worst week in six years.

The chipmaker’s file gained its cause on Friday and ends the week without the company’s answer. Nvidia closed at $125.53, down $20.45, or 14.01 percent, in the chip quote account filed below, a seventh straight lower close; on the week the shares fell 22.7 percent in the year account and 22.9 percent in the futures account, their worst week since October 2008, and the company’s market value stood at about $3.03 trillion, below Alphabet at about $3.25 trillion, in the value account filed below. The fall steepened after 2:15 p.m., when Reuters reported that Securities and Exchange Commission enforcement staff are scrutinising potential accounting issues at the company, on the word of two people briefed on the matter, in the inquiry account filed below. The Journal had reported the probe’s existence on Tuesday without its focus. The reporting around the inquiry centres on the company’s change last year in geographic revenue reporting—from billing addresses to customer headquarters—which removed Singapore from the breakdown as sales booked there rose toward half of global revenue, some $104 billion for 2025 in the probe account filed below; whether that change is inside the inquiry’s scope is not established in any account in the file. The Commission declined to comment; the company did not immediately respond; no charges stand in the file, and an inquiry is not a finding. The board’s position, stated Tuesday by its chairman, stands unaltered at midnight: the board does not intend to reinstate Mr. Huang, and the search firm Heidrick & Struggles is engaged to find a permanent chief executive, with Ms. Kress as interim. Against it stands the President’s word on Friday, in the Washington file below. Settled: the week, the correction, and the inquiry’s reported focus. Open: the inquiry’s scope, the company’s answer, and the succession.

Washington at Midnight: One Term for the Guardrails, and Two Tellings of the Huang Question

The noon conference’s one announcement gained its content on Friday from the Treasury Secretary, speaking after the return from Shenzhen. President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in military decisions that use artificial intelligence, and that no major military operation should be launched without a human being involved, Mr. Bessent told CNBC, in the Secretary’s account above, calling the agreement among the trip’s major achievements and saying it would stand apart from the two countries’ competition in the technology. That is the whole of the guardrails’ stated content at midnight: no text, no timetable, and no negotiating agency stands in the file, and no confirmation in Beijing’s own words stands in the file either; an earlier embassy statement carried in the week’s file, that the two sides should strengthen communication and keep the technology under human control, is the nearest parallel. Mr. Bessent added the chip position in the same interview: the H200 remains the most advanced chip China may purchase under licence, and Chinese orders for it have been few. The President’s own conference stands as the evening printed it—the trip a resounding success, data centres to be built at home and penalised abroad, only older chips for China—in the conference account filed below.

On the chipmaker’s former chief, Friday produced two tellings that do not meet, and the desk prints both. The President said he had discussed Mr. Huang with President Xi, that President Xi agreed Mr. Huang was a brilliant man, and that Mr. Huang had made some bad decisions: “I would like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back&hellip;we’re a country of second chances,” in the conference report filed below. Mr. Bessent said the allegations involving Mr. Huang did not come up in the bilateral meeting, in the Secretary’s account. The board’s stated position, against both tellings, is the one in the New York file: no reinstatement intended, a search under way. Settled: the guardrails’ one term, stated by the Secretary. Open: their text, Beijing’s confirmation, and which telling of the Huang conversation is the record.

Kyiv at Midnight: Nine Dead, Restricted Traffic, and an Answer Made of Words

The night’s count finished where the evening left it, and the midnight file records the finished figures and the day’s military reading together. At least nine people were killed: seven in Kyiv and two in other regions, in the latest account above, with the injured at 30 across Ukraine in the Interior Minister’s count and 17 in Kyiv in the mayor’s; a second full account puts the dead at at least eight, six in Kyiv and two in Lviv—the desk prints the spread in the Cocked Hat. The package stands at 27 ballistic missiles, 84 cruise missiles and 404 drones, the largest of November, in the assessment above, with air defences downing or suppressing three ballistic missiles, 79 cruise missiles and 380 drones and strikes recorded at 23 locations, in the latest account. The strike hit the Western Ukrainian 750-kilovolt substation, the largest in Europe, and forced the nuclear plants to reduce generation, with parts of Kyiv and ten regions without electricity, in the same account. Ukraine’s own strikes in the same hours hit three Russian ballistic missile launchers, destroying one, in the strike account filed below, and the Druzhba pumping station in Tatarstan on Thursday, damaging three storage tanks, in the latest account.

In Kyiv the repair advanced a step past the evening file. Traffic across the Podilskyi crossing was restored at about 3 p.m. local time, in the latest account, and the assessment records restricted traffic resumed across the damaged bridges generally; the Darnytskyi assessment continues and the Pivdennyi remains partly restricted, in the same account. In Poland the day produced the alliance’s fullest statement of what it did and did not do. Two Kh-101 missiles came down at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik nad Sanem and a jet-powered drone, possibly a Geran-5, at Molodycz, with no damage at any of the three, in the assessment; as many as 11 missiles and drones in Ukrainian airspace were tracked as potential threats to Poland’s, Polish, Swedish and Dutch aircraft were scrambled, and Poland and the alliance did not try to down the missiles and the drone because the conditions did not meet the rules of engagement, the operational commander said, in the same account. Prime Minister Tusk called the falls an intentional provocation; the Secretary General condemned the attack and the violation; France’s foreign minister called for a meeting of the Security Council; and Estonia will close its road border crossings with Russia on December 1, in the provocation account filed below and the latest account. President Zelensky’s reading stands against the week’s diplomacy, as the evening printed it: the attempt in Shenzhen to redraw the world had failed. UNICEF’s figures for the year stand beside the night’s: 1,144 children killed or injured between January and October. Settled: the count, the reopening in restricted form, and the non-interception, stated plainly by the commander who ordered it. Open: the Darnytskyi damage, the Council’s meeting, and the alliance’s answer beyond words.

The Gulf at Midnight: A Tanker Unnamed, a Weapon in Dispute, and Two Counts That Do Not Meet

Friday’s strike in the strait ends the day as it began it in the file: a ship with no name. A tanker on an outbound transit was struck on its port bow by an unknown projectile at about 1500 UTC, eight nautical miles north of Khasab, and its company security officer reported a fire on board, under Warning 214-26, in the fire account filed below; no casualties and no environmental impact were reported, and no later account in the file names the vessel, gives its flag or cargo, or reports the fire’s end. The Guards said the tanker caught fire after hitting a mine on an unauthorised transit; the mine explanation has not been independently verified, in the tanker account filed below. The week’s run now has a count of its own: seven strikes involving six vessels in the Gulf in the period, four of them tankers hit within 13 nautical miles of Khasab over three days, including the Tara Gas, attacked twice, in the surge account filed below, which puts maritime security incidents at their highest weekly level since mid-October.

The strait’s traffic ends the week with two counts that cannot both be the traffic. Eight commercial ships crossed on Friday as of 1802 UTC, five inbound and three outbound, two of them tankers, and 47 in the last seven days, an average of 6.7 a day against 84.8 before the crisis, in the strait count filed below. The Maritime Trade Operations agency’s weekly overview reports 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits over the preceding seven days, down from 139 and 169 the week before, in the surge account—263 crossings against the strait count’s 47. The desk prints the disagreement in the Cocked Hat without resolving it: the two instruments are not counting the same strait in the same way, and the file does not say how either counts. Oil’s week closed against its day: Brent settled Friday at $92.57 a barrel, up 0.64 percent, and December West Texas Intermediate at $83.98, up 0.93 percent, in the settlement account filed below, while the week’s readings put Brent down near 5 percent and the December contract down 6.5 percent, a third straight weekly decline, in the weekly account filed below, and United States crude futures down 19.2 percent for November, in the futures account. The OPEC+ ministers meet November 29. Settled: the strike, the settlement, and the week’s direction in oil. Open: the tanker’s name and state, the weapon, the true count of the strait, and the missing men of the week’s earlier ships.

France and Spain at Midnight: A Law Passed, a Referral Promised, and a Verdict Confirmed

France’s file closed in the Senate and reopens at the Council. Senators gave final approval to the law presuming that police officers who use their weapons are acting lawfully, by 205 votes to 110, in the Paris account filed below; the law gives an officer who has shot someone the benefit of the doubt unless there is proof to the contrary. The Interior Minister, Mr. Nu&ntilde;ez, supports it as protection for officers in dangerous conditions; the United Nations special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions wrote ahead of the vote that the burden of disproving lawfulness should not fall on victims and their families; and the left-wing groups plan to refer the law to the Constitutional Council in a last effort to halt it, in the same account. No filing of that referral stands in the file at midnight: the referral is promised, not yet made. Settled: the vote and the text. Open: the referral, and the Council’s word.

Spain’s verdict, split on Thursday night, stands confirmed on two instruments at midnight, as the evening printed it: Mr. Feij&oacute;o the perceived winner of the debate, 51 percent to 29 percent in the Sigma Dos poll and 43 percent to 33 percent in the 40dB poll, before an audience of 10.2 million, in the Madrid account filed below. The standing instruments show an advantage for a bloc of the People’s Party and Vox; no post-debate voting-intention poll stands in the file. The second debate stands agreed for about November 26, and Spain votes November 29. Settled: the verdict. Open: whether it moves the vote.

The Air at Midnight: The Week Ends Without Its Root Cause

The week’s Washington promise stands unkept at the midnight stamp, as it stood at the evening’s. The Federal Aviation Administration said on Thursday that the government expected to announce this week the root cause of the November 13 ground stop; Friday’s file contains no announcement, and the week that contained the promise has now closed. The narrowed field stands as the evening printed it: a radar site at Amarillo, Texas, and a radio site at El Dorado, Arkansas, where the contractor L3Harris had been installing a new router in a copper-to-fibre upgrade; data flooding the network at 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilising 17 of the 22 en route centres, in the funding account filed below; the two routers at a laboratory in Florida for examination, and no evidence of a cyberattack, in the week account filed below. Secretary Duffy’s formulation remains the file’s firmest: the installation or the router was the bad actor. The installations stand paused and the new routers’ broadcasting function disabled. Congress is questioning the Secretary’s $50 billion modernisation request while the inquiry proceeds, in the funding account, and the Senate Commerce Committee is owed its technical answers by November 23—the first date of the Thanksgiving travel week, which now stands directly ahead of the unanswered question. Settled: the equipment, the two sites, and the precaution. Open: the root cause itself, a week and a day outstanding.

The Week Ahead: A Short Market Week, a Certification, and Two Votes

Saturday carries the paper’s Culture Feature, in the FT Weekend manner, and the Overnight Watch collects at 0400. The futures reopen Sunday at 1800 Eastern. The week ahead is short in New York—Dell’s earnings, the second estimate of the product, and the PCE reading, with the markets closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and closing at 1300 on Friday—and full elsewhere: the Senate Commerce Committee’s technical answers on the ground stop, due November 23; Alaska’s certification on November 25; Spain’s second debate, about November 26, and its vote on November 29; the OPEC+ ministers on November 29; the French left’s referral of the police law to the Constitutional Council; the Federal Reserve’s decision on December 8 and 9; the end of government funding after December 11; and the Bank of Japan’s decision on December 18. The Midnight Watch collects at 0000.

The Cocked Hat

Where the day’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Anthropic’s close: $88.30, down 9.1 percent, in the close account, against $88.91, down 8.50 percent, in the quote account, on the same session’s open of $89.86, high of $92.56 and low of $83.05. On Nvidia’s close: $125.53, down 14.01 percent, in the chip quote account, against $125.84, down 13.8 percent, in the slide account carried in the evening file. On Nvidia’s week: down 22.7 percent in the year account, 22.9 percent in the futures account, and 23 percent in the Journal’s weekly wrap. On the fear gauge: 38.50 at its week’s high in the year account, 35.89 at the close in the pulse account. On Kyiv’s dead: nine in the latest account, seven in Kyiv and two elsewhere; at least eight in the blitz account carried in the evening file, six in Kyiv and two in Lviv. On the injured: 30 across Ukraine in the Interior Minister’s count, at least 28 in the strike account, and 17 in Kyiv in the mayor’s. On the bridges: traffic restored across the Podilskyi crossing and partly restricted on the Pivdennyi in the latest account, against restricted traffic resumed across the damaged bridges generally in the assessment. On the Huang conversation: discussed with President Xi, in the conference report; not raised in the bilateral, in the Secretary’s account. On the strait’s week: 47 crossings in the strait count, against 263 in the Maritime Trade Operations agency’s weekly overview—115 outbound and 148 inbound. On oil: a settlement of $92.57 for Brent and $83.98 for December West Texas in the settlement account, against $91.31 and $82.85 at 1414 GMT in the weekly account. Inside the triangle is where the day honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

### The House Took Fifty Years to Grow Hands: X10 and the Relay Era, the Sensor Stack, the Luxury Tier, and the Humanoid Machines of 2026

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-20T23:15:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-20-physical-ai.html

Special Report

 Physical AI, Filed From the Record

 Objective

 The House Took Fifty Years to Grow Hands: X10 and the Relay Era, the Sensor Stack, the Luxury Tier, and the Humanoid Machines of 2026

 Home automation began in 1975 as a signal riding the power line to a relay: the house could be switched and could report nothing back. Fifty years of development then gave the house senses—microphones, cameras, a laser that maps the floor—and a nervous system of mesh radios and voice assistants, without giving it any way to act on what it sensed. The luxury tier wired whole estates at installed costs running to $300,000, and every published scope in that tier is environmental: light, shade, climate, sound, gates. No platform at any price lists the ability to pick an object up. Physical AI is the name for the correction now arriving: generalist machines with arms and hands, priced from $4,900 to unpublished, trained in simulation and on human video. The 2026 ledger of that arrival is narrower than its announcements. The one consumer humanoid with an order page, 1X’s NEO, has a factory in full production and, as of November 13, 2026, zero verified deliveries to a paying customer. The strongest commercial record in the field belongs to a warehouse machine moving totes under a multi-year service contract. And across every serious estimate, the actuators account for half to three-fifths of what a humanoid costs to build. The record, era by era and machine by machine, follows.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 2315 ET, Friday, November 20, 2026.

The Record in Brief

The arc divides into three eras. In the first, X10, developed by Pico Electronics in 1975 and sold from 1978, sent commands over the house wiring as bursts at the zero crossings of the alternating current—one-way, unacknowledged, unauthenticated. A controller could order a lamp on; nothing in the protocol could confirm that the lamp was on, and a neighbor on the same distribution transformer could receive the signal. In the second era, the house acquired senses in sequence: the learning thermostat in 2011, the voice assistant in 2014, the doorbell camera, the LiDAR vacuum that mapped the home in 2016, and the Matter standard in 2022 to bind them. Through 2020 the flagship stack was eyes, ears, and a floor-bound puck—perception complete, manipulation absent. The era’s architecture risk has a date: April 15, 2022, when Insteon’s servers shut down without notice and hub-dependent homes went dark. The third era is the present one, and its machines are countable. 1X’s NEO, at $20,000 or $499 a month, is the only humanoid a consumer can order; its Hayward factory entered full-scale production on April 30, 2026, and the verified count of units delivered to a paying customer as of November 13, 2026 is zero, with early output routed to internal testing and a company statement pointing to first shipments in December. Tesla’s Optimus is in early production at Fremont, is not for sale at any price, and is targeted at outside deliveries around the end of 2027. Figure’s Figure 03 works in BMW plants; Boston Dynamics’ entire 2026 Atlas production is committed to Hyundai and Google DeepMind; Unitree’s machines are orderable today, the R1 from $4,900. Underneath the machines, two ledgers govern. The hardware ledger: actuators and drive components run at roughly 50 to 60 percent of a humanoid’s bill of materials on every sourced estimate—Schaeffler at about 50 percent, Morgan Stanley at 56, Hyundai Mobis at 60. The software ledger: the shipping reasoning stack is NVIDIA’s Isaac GR00T line, now at N1.7, trained on 20,854 hours of human egocentric video and in simulation, where the verified compressions are specific—42 years of a single robot’s experience in about 32 hours of compute in 2021, about 10 years in two hours in 2025, and 140 simulated years of self-play accumulated by Skild AI’s soccer policy in September 2026. There is no product named GR00T 2. The record follows.

1975: A Signal Riding the Power Line

X10 was developed in 1975 by Pico Electronics of Glenrothes, Scotland, and named for a plain reason: it was Pico’s tenth project. Products reached the market in 1978 through a partnership with BSR, opening with a 16-channel command console, a lamp module, and an appliance module. The signaling is documented to the half-cycle. The carrier is 120 kHz, sent as bursts at the zero crossings of the 50 or 60 Hz mains waveform; a 1 ms burst at a zero crossing is a logic 1, its absence a logic 0, and each bit is followed by its complement in the next half-cycle. Addressing is a 4-bit house code, letters A through P, plus a unit code from 1 to 16—256 possible addresses—and a frame carries a start code, the house code, and a key code holding either a unit number or a function: On, Off, Dim, Bright. A complete frame, transmitted twice with gaps, takes roughly a second.

The protocol’s blindness is structural, not incidental. Base X10 is one-way and fire-and-forget: no acknowledgment that a command arrived, no confirmation that a load switched. Two-way modules able to answer a Status Request were a later, minority addition. The failure modes are equally specific: powerline noise from motors, televisions, and switching power supplies swamps the 120 kHz signal; some devices act as signal suckers and absorb it; split-phase wiring strands a signal on one leg unless a phase coupler is fitted at the panel; and signals travel to a neighbor sharing the same distribution transformer, because the protocol carries no authentication and no encryption. The system reached the personal computer early—the CP-290 interface dates to the 1980s—and the late-1990s tinkering culture anchored on the FireCracker CM17A, a transmit-only serial-port radio dongle relayed onto the powerline through a transceiver, documented in hobbyist hands on machines as small as a 6502. The mainstream face of the era was not X10 at all: it was the Clapper, Joseph Enterprises’ sound-activated switch, famous through television advertising from the mid-to-late 1980s, while X10 remained a hobbyist system. The first era’s whole capability, stated plainly: a house that could be ordered, in the dark, and could not answer.

The Sensor Era: Eyes, Ears, and a Floor-Bound Puck

The second era added senses one at a time, and the dates form a single sequence. TiVo shipped its first DVR on March 31, 1999, and defined the connected living room of the 2000s; it discontinued its DVR hardware in October 2025. Sonos, founded in August 2002, introduced its wireless multiroom ZonePlayer line in January 2005, the template for app-era home audio—still without any manipulation capability. The mesh-radio layer arrived in the same decade: the Zigbee Alliance in 2002, the Z-Wave Alliance in 2005, and Philips Hue made Zigbee consumer-visible in 2012. The Nest Learning Thermostat was released on October 25, 2011, and reset consumer expectations for design and learning behavior; Google acquired Nest Labs in January 2014 for $3.2 billion. SmartThings launched on Kickstarter in 2012 and was acquired by Samsung in 2014. Home Assistant was started by Paulus Schoutsen on September 17, 2013, as a personal project to interface Philips Hue lights, published on GitHub that November under Apache 2.0, with local control and privacy as founding principles.

Amazon Echo was first released on November 6, 2014, to Prime members, with general release in June 2015; the first Google Home speaker followed on November 4, 2016. Ring’s original Video Doorbell dates to December 2012, and Amazon acquired Ring in 2018. LiDAR home mapping arrived with the Xiaomi Mi Robot Vacuum, built by Roborock and announced in August 2016, its laser distance sensor mapping the home as it cleaned; Roborock’s own-brand S5 followed in 2018. Matter, announced as Project Connected Home over IP in December 2019 by Amazon, Apple, Google, and the Zigbee Alliance, reached version 1.0 on October 4, 2022; Matter 1.2, in October 2023, added major appliances and robot vacuums. By 2020 the flagship consumer stack was complete and its limit was exact: Echo and Google Home for ears, Ring for eyes, a LiDAR puck for the floor—and nothing in the stack could move an object from one place to another. The era’s warning case is dated April 15, 2022, when Insteon’s servers shut down abruptly and hub-dependent homes were bricked without notice: the ambient house, rented from a cloud, could be repossessed by a server shutdown. The second era’s capability, stated as plainly as the first: a house that could see, hear, and report—and could not act.

The Luxury Tier: A Quarter of a Million Dollars, No Hands

Above the consumer tier, the same fifty years produced a dealer-locked luxury market. Crestron was founded by engineer George Feldstein in Rockleigh, New Jersey—the obituary record has him leaving his job and starting the business in 1969, while the company’s reference entries give a 1972 founding date; both dates stand in the record, attributed. By 1990 Crestron had over 100 employees and roughly $5 million in sales, serving luxury homes, boardrooms, and institutions. Its control-system rival AMX was founded in 1982 in Richardson, Texas. The 1990 state of the art divided exactly as the market still divides: a consumer tier of X10 Powerhouse modules, timers, and the CP-290, and a luxury tier of hardwired Crestron and early Lutron HomeWorks-class systems—wall keypads, dedicated touch panels, programmed per house.

The present tier’s terms are published by its own installers. All four flagship platforms—Crestron, Control4, Savant, and Lutron HomeWorks—require certified-dealer programming; homeowners cannot reprogram their own systems, and installers state this plainly. Installed costs, from integrators’ published ranges: a Hudson Valley integrator puts average projects at $30,000 to $200,000 and large estates at $50,000 to $250,000; an Atlanta integrator’s 2026 table gives Control4 at $10,000 to $50,000 and above, Savant at $15,000 to $75,000 and above, and Crestron Home at $40,000 to $150,000 and above; a Maryland integrator prices estate-scale work at $75,000 to $250,000 and above; a New York Lutron installer puts HomeWorks projects from around $50,000, commonly between $80,000 and $300,000. And the scopes are uniform. Every one of these installers’ published scopes is environmental and electrical—lighting and shades, climate, distributed audio and video, security and cameras, gates, pool and spa. No luxury platform lists any physical-manipulation capability. A $250,000 Crestron house can dim to 2700K and lower its shades on a geofence, and it cannot pick a wet towel off the floor. The last inch of the automated house—the distance between sensing a thing and moving it—is the distance the third era exists to close.

The Consumer Machine: NEO, Its Order Page, and Its Empty Delivery Ledger

1X’s NEO is the one humanoid a consumer can order, and its specification, per 1X’s own order page, is complete: 5 feet 6 inches tall, 66 pounds, lifts 154 pounds, carries 55, arm payload 18; 75 degrees of freedom in total, the hands at 22 each on the order page—a figure 1X’s July 9, 2026 announcement of a new hand supersedes at 25 per hand, 22 in fingers and palm plus 3 at the wrist, force-controlled with tactile and shear sensing; the order page appears stale, and both figures stand dated. The body is a soft shell of custom 3D lattice polymer with no pinch points, low-inertia tendon drives rated 95 percent backdrivable, hands rated IP68 and body IP44, four beamforming microphones, dual 8.85-megapixel 90 Hz stereo fisheye cameras, and compute on NVIDIA Jetson Thor at up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS. The order page disagrees with itself on the battery—842 watt-hours in the specification table, 0.75 kilowatt-hours in the same page’s FAQ—with runtime given as about four hours either way. NEO runs Redwood, 1X’s vision-language-action model, introduced June 10, 2025 and trained on teleoperated and autonomous episodes from 1X’s EVE and NEO robots; the company also lists a 1X World Model dated January 12, 2026.

The commercial record divides into production and delivery, and the two do not meet. Preorders opened October 28, 2025, at $20,000 outright or $499 a month, against a $200 deposit; the order banner calls the deposit fully refundable, and the pre-order terms limit a full refund to 14 days after the Order Invitation email—the terms, not the banner, are the record. 1X took more than 10,000 orders in the first days, by the company’s account. The Hayward factory began full-scale production on April 30, 2026, at a stated capacity of 10,000 robots a year, with early output prioritized to internal testing. As of November 13, 2026, the count of NEO units verifiably delivered to a paying customer is zero: The Information reported the absence of deliveries on August 27, 2026, Reuters carried it the same day, and 1X has issued no delay announcement and no first-delivery post. A company briefing carried by RobotToday has B&oslash;rnich pointing to shipments beginning in December 2026; that line stands as announced, not as delivered. Production is not delivery, and the delivery ledger is the one that is empty.

What a delivered NEO would do in 2026 is also on the record, and it includes a person. Expert Mode, 1X’s teleoperation bridge, works as follows per the company’s launch briefing and FAQ: the owner books a session in the app and must approve it; a United States-based 1X employee pilots the robot wearing a VR headset; people in the home can be blurred in the operator’s feed; owners can set no-go zones the robot respects even under teleoperation; the ear-ring light shows when a session is active; and each session doubles as training data. In July 2026 reporting, the Wall Street Journal’s Joanna Stern found every household task in her session driven by a teleoperator, and 1X is explicit that teleoperation is part of the product at launch. None of the safeguards has been independently audited, for the documented reason: the robots are not yet in customers’ homes.

The Industrial Machines: BMW, Fremont, Hyundai, and the Tote Line

Figure’s record is the fullest deployment file in the field. Figure 02, the predecessor, completed an 11-month deployment at BMW’s Plant Spartanburg loading sheet metal: 10-hour shifts, more than 90,000 parts loaded, over 1,250 runtime hours, contributing to more than 30,000 BMW X3 vehicles, with over 99 percent successful placement per shift; the fleet was retired in November 2025. Figure 03, unveiled October 9, 2025—173 centimeters, about 61 kilograms, a 2.3 kilowatt-hour battery, palm cameras, fingertip sensors detecting 3 grams, wireless charging—is built at Figure’s BotQ plant at a stated 12,000 units a year of capacity; over 350 units had been delivered by April 2026, and since June 30, 2026 one has run parts sequencing at Spartanburg under Helix 02. A second agreement, with Catalyst Brands on May 26, 2026, covers distribution centers. Figure publishes no price, and consumer deliveries are zero. Helix 02, released in January 2026, is a single vision-language-action network controlling the whole body from pixels: its System 0 layer of 10 million parameters, trained on over 1,000 hours of human motion data and running at 1 kHz, replaced 109,504 lines of hand-written C++, under a System 1 visuomotor policy and a System 2 semantic layer; its showpiece was a four-minute autonomous dishwasher load and unload.

Tesla’s Optimus stands at the opposite entry from NEO: production announced, sale absent. On its third-quarter earnings call, October 21, 2026, Tesla said early production has begun on a high-volume line at Fremont, in the space where Model S and X were built until May 2026—some reporting dates the line’s start to late August 2026; the October call is the announcement of record. The line is designed for about a million robots a year; reaching 20,000 a week will take at least a year on a slow, bumpy ramp. The first units go to Tesla’s internal Optimus Academy; outside deliveries are expected around the end of 2027, industrial customers first. The $20,000 to $30,000 figure attached to Optimus is a long-term cost target, not a price: Tesla publishes no price and takes no reservations, and Musk denied a December 2026 reservation opening on October 30, 2026. The third-generation robot has never had a formal public unveil.

Boston Dynamics’ Atlas, in its product version, was unveiled at CES on January 5, 2026, and is in production at the company’s Boston headquarters: 1.9 meters, 90 kilograms, 56 degrees of freedom, 50 kilograms of instant lift and 30 sustained, a 2.3-meter reach, IP67 sealing, about four hours per battery with autonomous swap in about three minutes. The entire 2026 production run is committed to two customers—Hyundai’s Robotics Metaplant Application Center in Georgia, opened September 21, 2026, and Google DeepMind. The first customer outside the Hyundai group is planned for 2027, and Hyundai’s production-line deployment from 2028. Boston Dynamics publishes no price; a figure of about $130,000 to $140,000 was relayed to analysts at CES and reported through a Samsung Securities analyst in the Boston Globe, and it stands in the record as single-relay sourcing, printed with that caution attached. Apptronik’s Apollo has run pilots at Mercedes-Benz’s Digital Factory Campus in Berlin and lab evaluation with GXO; Apollo 2 was unveiled June 30, 2026, for task-data collection fleets, and the company puts production versions in 2027 and beyond, on $935 million raised at about a $5 billion valuation.

The strongest commercial record in the category belongs to Agility Robotics’ Digit, and it is a service record, not a sales record: a multi-year robots-as-a-service contract at a GXO-operated Spanx facility in Georgia—the first formal commercial humanoid deployment—moving totes from mobile robots to conveyors, with more than 100,000 totes moved and a claimed 65,000-plus fleet operational hours across nine customer sites, among them Amazon, Schaeffler, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and Mercado Libre; one count puts about 250 commercial Digit units in service. Unitree holds the field’s price floor. The G1, launched in May 2024 at $16,000 maker-direct, held that price for roughly 17 months before stepping down once, to $13,500 in a store capture dated December 24, 2025; as of August 2026 it is orderable but backordered, with United States dealer prices around $17,990. The R1, introduced July 25, 2025 from $5,900, listed from $4,900 maker-direct by September 2026 and actually ships—the first walking humanoid under $5,000 at a real checkout. Clone Robotics’ Protoclone is the field’s outlier, and its honest record is narrower than its pitch: a musculoskeletal android of 206-bone polymer skeleton and more than 1,000 Myofiber artificial muscles, shown in 2025 videos actuating while suspended from a frame; the current prototype runs on compressed air, water hydraulics is the production plan, and no footage shows it bearing its own weight, standing, or walking.

Hands, and the Actuator Ledger

The hand is where the category’s claims meet a specification sheet. LinkerBot’s Linker Hand O30 is a five-fingered direct-drive dexterous hand with 20 fully active degrees of freedom—every joint independently motor-driven, no tendons or linkages—at 730 grams, a 30-kilogram rated payload, an integrated 6-by-11 tactile array across the fingertips, CAN-FD control at 500 Hz, and plus-or-minus 0.2 millimeter repeatability, per the manufacturer’s manual V1.0 of July 14, 2026. The maker’s further claim, that the O30 is the only full direct-drive dexterous hand in mass production, stands as the maker’s claim, not as an established fact; the specifications are the verified part. The supply chain behind the joints is documented at the name level. Harmonic Drive Systems of Japan is the incumbent strain-wave gear maker whose name became the generic term; China’s Leaderdrive sold 425,158 harmonic reducers in 2025, up 72 percent year on year, supplying AgiBot and UBTech—the desk prints the unit sales and drops the market-share percentages, because the sourced share figures conflict beyond reconciliation. Green Harmonic is the other Chinese reducer name, reported as a second source for Optimus. Schaeffler sells integrated rotary actuators, planetary roller screws, and bearings into humanoid programs; Hyundai Mobis supplies Atlas’s actuators. An Optimus-class machine is reported to carry about 14 to 16 planetary roller screws, about 14 harmonic reducers, roughly 20 coreless motors per hand, and over 40 servo motors.

The cost consequence is the actuator ledger, and every sourced estimate puts the same weight in the same place. Schaeffler puts actuators at about 50 percent of a typical humanoid’s bill of materials. Morgan Stanley’s teardown estimate for an Optimus-class machine is about 56 percent of a roughly $55,000 bill of materials. Hyundai Mobis puts the figure at about 60 percent of material cost. Bank of America’s projected 2030 split—linear 27 percent, rotary 24—sums to 51 percent. The range across the record is therefore 50 to 60 percent: the majority of what a humanoid costs to build is the machinery of moving. The electronics industry priced its entry against that ledger on March 16, 2026, when Infineon, NXP, and STMicroelectronics all announced partnerships with NVIDIA to sell humanoid hardware around the Jetson Thor platform, with Infineon anticipating about $500 of parts content per robot. Analyst shipment totals carry the same instruction to print the firm with the figure: Goldman Sachs estimated about 75,000 humanoids shipped worldwide in 2026; Omdia counted 13,318 shipped in 2025 and ranked AgiBot first at 5,168 units, a figure Unitree disputes with its own count of more than 5,500; a May 2026 industry memo put only about 7,000 to 8,000 humanoids as operational worldwide. The spread is the record.

The Software Stack: World Models, Vision-Language-Action Models, and Simulated Years

The stack beneath the machines consolidated in public on a single day. At CES on January 5, 2026, NVIDIA announced Cosmos Transfer 2.5 and Cosmos Predict 2.5, open world models for synthetic data generation and policy evaluation in simulation; Cosmos Reason 2, an open reasoning vision-language model; Isaac GR00T N1.6; Isaac Lab-Arena, an open-source evaluation framework; and the OSMO edge-to-cloud workflow framework. The current GR00T is Isaac GR00T N1.7: early access April 17, 2026, general availability by November 2026—a 3-billion-parameter open reasoning VLA, commercially licensed, whose System 2 backbone is Cosmos-Reason2-2B and whose pretraining, called EgoScale, used 20,854 hours of human egocentric video across more than 20 task categories. NVIDIA claims the first dexterity scaling law for the field: going from 1,000 to 20,000 hours of human video more than doubles average task completion. No product named GR00T 2 exists in NVIDIA’s newsroom, model cards, or repositories; the line runs N1, N1.6, N1.7. The System 1 and System 2 split is concrete in the shipping stacks, not diagrammatic: GR00T N1.7 pairs its reasoning backbone with a diffusion-transformer action head, and Figure’s Helix 02 pairs a semantic layer with the 1 kHz learned whole-body layer that replaced hand-written control code. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, released September 3, 2026, is a general frontier language model; no NVIDIA, Figure, or 1X source places it inside a robot control stack, and the reasoning backbones actually shipping in robots are the two named above.

Simulation is where the training years come from, and the compressions are documented at specific scales with dates. Newton, an open-source GPU-accelerated physics engine co-developed by NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and Disney Research and managed by the Linux Foundation, went beta September 29, 2025 and reached 1.0 in March 2026, with native integration in Isaac Lab 3.0—itself in general availability on October 20, 2026. NVIDIA’s GTC 2026 figures claim 252-times acceleration for humanoid locomotion and 475-times for in-hand manipulation against MJX baselines; those are vendor numbers and are printed as such. The experience compressions: NVIDIA’s Isaac Gym work trained a dexterous hand policy in about 32 hours of compute equivalent to 42 years of a single robot’s experience, in 2021; NVIDIA’s 2025 locomotion demonstrations compressed about 10 years into two hours across thousands of parallel simulated robots; and Skild AI’s soccer policy accumulated 140 simulated years of self-play in Isaac Sim before transfer to a physical robot, in September 2026. The mechanism is uniform—thousands of parallel instances on one GPU—and the 140-year figure belongs to the Skild case alone. Egocentric human video is the second training source, now at production scale: GR00T N1.7’s 20,854 hours is the headline instance, and Helix 02’s System 0 was trained on over 1,000 hours of human motion data. The academic edge of the same method is HumanX, from HKUST and Shanghai AI Laboratory, which transferred 10 skills across five domains, basketball to reactive fighting, zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1. Two measures of NVIDIA’s position circulate with different denominators, both printed labeled: ABI Research, carried by Reuters on March 16, 2026, estimated NVIDIA’s platform is used in more than 80 percent of humanoid robots—a platform-presence estimate—while a single thinner report puts Jetson’s share of edge-AI-chip revenue at about 39 percent, flagged as directional by its carrier.

The Open Tabletop: What a Hobbyist Needs in November 2026

The bottom of the stack is open, cheap, and documented. The tabletop standard is the SO-101, a six-degree-of-freedom open-source arm from The Robot Studio and Hugging Face’s LeRobot line—the SO-100 of October 2024, the SO-101 of April 2025, Apache 2.0—built from six Feetech STS3215 servos. Parts run about $122 for one follower arm and about $230 for a leader-follower pair before printing the frame; assembled kits sell for roughly $249 to $316. GR00T N1.7’s documented hardware floors set the compute requirement: inference needs one GPU with 16 GB or more of memory—the README names the RTX 4090, L40, H100, Jetson AGX Thor, Jetson AGX Orin, and DGX Spark—and fine-tuning needs 40 GB or more, with H100 or L40 nodes recommended. A 16 GB consumer card therefore runs a trained policy locally, and a Jetson developer kit runs it at the edge on hardware like the SO-101. Jetson Thor has been generally available since August 2025: Blackwell-based, up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS in a 40-to-130-watt envelope, 128 GB of memory on the module, a $3,499 developer kit, and the T5000 production module reported at $2,999 in volume. The hobbyist’s arm now runs the same model family as the factory humanoid, on a card that fits in a desktop.

What the Record Shows

The fifty-year record closes on four instruments. A protocol: X10, which could command and could not confirm, and whose blindness was never repaired, only succeeded. A scope list: the luxury tier’s, environmental from top to bottom at prices to $300,000, the documentary proof that the automated house’s missing faculty was never sensing or switching but handling. An order page: exactly one for a consumer humanoid, behind which stands a factory in full production and a delivery ledger that reads zero—production and delivery are separate facts, and in November 2026 they have not yet met. And a bill of materials: half to three-fifths actuators on every sourced estimate, which is why the field’s center of gravity sits in gear factories in Japan and China as much as in model laboratories. The machines that work today work in factories and warehouses, under service contracts, at unpublished prices. The machine that can be ordered for a home arrives, when it arrives, with a person at the controls for the tasks its software has not mastered. The record shows the hands built, priced, and in production—and the delivery column still empty.

### Jensen Huang Resigns at Nvidia; Google Launches New AI Chips; Two Riemann Hypothesis Proof Claims; The Humanoid Robot Ledger

Filed as: Special Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-20T18:30:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-20-besides-anthropic.html

Special Report

 The Week in Technology, Filed From the Record

 Objective

 Jensen Huang Resigns at Nvidia; Google Launches New AI Chips; Two Riemann Hypothesis Proof Claims; The Humanoid Robot Ledger

 Four stories carried the week in technology outside the Anthropic announcements, the service outages, and the GTA VI launch. Nvidia’s board accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang, the founder who built the company into the largest in the industry, after reporting on two extramarital affairs, one of them with a businesswoman at a firm under investigation for smuggling restricted Nvidia chips into China. Two days before the resignation was accepted, Google expanded its eighth-generation TPU line with two systems aimed at the market Nvidia leads. On Friday, a mathematician at Anthropic posted a claim, made working with Claude, to have proved the Riemann Hypothesis, and hours later a second claim, an entirely human-written proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, was released after months of private vetting. And the humanoid robot, the week’s standing fourth story, resolves on inspection into a ledger of exactly one consumer order page. The record, story by story, follows.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1830 ET, Friday, November 20, 2026.

The Record in Brief

The week’s largest technology story is a departure. Nvidia’s board accepted Jen-Hsun Huang’s resignation as president, chief executive, and board member on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, effective immediately, and announced it on November 12 by press release and Form 8-K. Huang founded the company in 1993 and led it for 33 years to a peak valuation above $5.5 trillion. The reported cause is conduct: two extramarital affairs disclosed in reporting, one with a businesswoman whose firm is under investigation for smuggling restricted Nvidia chips into China and whom United States officials suspect was recruited by Chinese intelligence. Colette Kress, the executive vice president and chief financial officer, serves as interim chief executive while remaining chief financial officer; Harvey C. Jones became the board’s first chair. The company had no succession plan. Its shares opened down more than 10 percent on November 12; the full range of the reported fall is printed below, attributed, because the figure depends on the window measured. On November 9, two days before the board acted, Google launched the TPU 8tx and the TPU 8i Max, its third and fourth new TPU systems of the year. On Friday, November 20, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a four-page note claiming a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis made working with Claude, released as a Lean formalization in a 14-part archive; an MIT mathematician independently compiled the proof and put the chance that anything in the compilation is amiss at approximately zero, while the check that the formal statement is the hypothesis itself remained outstanding at filing. Hours later, the president of the American Mathematical Society released a competing, entirely human-written draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, vetted privately for months. The humanoid ledger stands as follows: one machine, 1X’s NEO, has a consumer order page, at $20,000 or $499 a month, and it works in 2026 with a human operator at the controls for the tasks its software has not mastered; Tesla’s Optimus is in early production and is sold at no price, because it is not for sale; Figure’s current machine works in BMW plants; Boston Dynamics’ 2026 Atlas production is committed to Hyundai and Google DeepMind; Unitree’s machines are orderable today as research platforms.

The Resignation: Accepted November 11, Announced November 12

The instrument is a Form 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission under Item 5.02, the departure of a principal officer. Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation on November 11, effective immediately; the company announced the transition on November 12. Kress holds the chief executive’s office on an interim basis during the board’s search and keeps the chief financial officer’s office at the same time. Jones’s appointment makes him the first person to hold the chairmanship as a separate office in the company’s history. Huang’s tenure ran from the founding in 1993 to this month: 33 years, ending at a company that had passed a $5.5 trillion peak valuation earlier this year, as The Register recorded in its account of the resignation. The Associated Press reported that the company had no succession plan. On Tuesday, November 17, Nvidia reported its third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings on the date previously scheduled, with Kress at the helm.

The Conduct Record

The reporting that preceded the resignation came in two disclosures. Reporting in late October, and again on November 11, disclosed two extramarital affairs. The first was with Alice Huang, no relation, a businesswoman at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm under investigation for smuggling restricted Nvidia chips into China; United States officials suspect she was recruited by Chinese intelligence. The second was with an Nvidia executive who reported to Huang. On Sunday, November 8, Huang admitted an affair and apologized to employees. The board’s first position, stated that week, was that it had “confidence” in him and “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” On November 11, after the second relationship was reported, the board reversed and accepted the resignation. CNN’s account records that the board’s own investigation into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort preceded the resignation. Le Monde placed the resignation against the midterm results: Democrats won both houses of Congress and are demanding stricter oversight of strategic exports to China.

The Fall in the Shares, Printed as a Range

The sources disagree on the size of the fall because they measured different windows, and the desk prints the range with its attributions rather than a single figure. The Wall Street Journal’s live coverage and CNN’s pre-market reporting put the shares down more than 10 percent at the open on November 12. The Associated Press, in the account carried by TechXplore, reported a 14 percent drop at the opening bell before the price stabilized. Le Monde put the after-hours price at $159, roughly a third below the early-October peak, with more than $2 trillion in market value gone. Each figure is the measure of its window: the pre-market indication, the opening print, the after-hours price against the October peak. The record supports the range and every attribution in it; it does not support collapsing the range into one number.

Google, Two Days Before the Fall

On November 9, two days before the board accepted the resignation, Google expanded its eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two systems, announced on the company’s blog and covered by TechCrunch on November 10. The TPU 8tx is built for secure and confidential inference: it pairs TPU 8t silicon with fifth-generation AMD EPYC host processors, and AMD’s SEV technology extends confidential-computing protection to the accelerator itself. The TPU 8i Max packages two TPU 8i chips in one system, doubling compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth, for workloads carrying massive context windows. The two launches brought Google to four new TPU systems in a single year. Barron’s framed the launch explicitly against Nvidia “grappling with an investigation into reports that its CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.” Google no longer keeps the machines in-house: nearly 100 customers use TPUs, and Reuters reported that Oracle will offer TPUs on its cloud from 2027. Google gave no prices and no availability dates for the two new systems.

Friday: A Claim on the Riemann Hypothesis

The third story is Anthropic-adjacent, and the desk files it flagged as such: it belongs to this record because the claim landed on Friday and because its verification status is a matter of public record, not because it clears the week’s exclusion. On Friday, November 20, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a four-page note on his personal website. Its first sentence is the claim: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.” The same method is claimed to settle the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. The proof was released as a formalization in Lean, the proof-assistant language, in a 14-part archive; there is no conventional paper, and Alpöge states that a full written argument would be extremely long and that he has not mastered all of the territory himself. He has worked with Claude on the problem since October 6, with key steps dated November 15. He consulted Dario Amodei before announcing, and acknowledged that the timing could be viewed cynically: Anthropic’s shares began trading on the Nasdaq on November 19, the day before the announcement. Scientific American and the Associated Press account carried by phys.org record the claim and its circumstances.

The Verification Ledger: Claimed, Compiled, Comparator Pending

A proof claim resolves in stages, and the record assigns each stage its own status. Claimed: the note and the 14-part Lean archive are public, as of Friday. Compiled: Andrew Sutherland of MIT independently compiled the Lean proof and reported the result in terms the desk prints in full: “The Lean proof has been compiled and independently rechecked by the Lean kernel with only the three standard axioms... Honestly the chance that anything is fishy here is approximately zero.” The compilation establishes that the formal argument checks, step by step, against the three standard axioms of the system. Comparator pending: the run that checks the formal statement itself—that the theorem the archive proves is the Riemann Hypothesis as mathematics states it, with no symbol redefined on the way in—had not been reported at filing; Scientific American put that check a matter of hours away. Publication and prize: the Clay Mathematics Institute’s million-dollar Millennium Prize requires formal publication, a process measured far beyond hours. The desk prints the stages separately because they are separate facts: a compiled proof of a statement is one record, and the identity of the statement is another, and at 1830 on Friday the first stood verified and the second stood open.

Hours after Alpöge’s announcement, a second claim entered the record from the opposite direction. Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society, released a draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written entirely by Alessandro Masullo, an independent mathematician, which had been under private vetting for months, with Stanford’s Brian Conrad among the vetters. Vakil’s circle had planned a year of quiet polishing at Stanford and released the draft early so the human result would not be eclipsed by the machine-assisted claim. The Masullo draft is not in Lean; its examination runs through conventional peer review and will take months. Scientific American and DataCamp record both claims and the order in which they landed: the machine’s proof, kernel-checked the same day, and the human’s proof, months from a verdict, on the same Friday.

The Humanoid Ledger: One Order Page

The fourth story is a frame before it is a product. Home automation has run in three eras. X10, from 1975, flipped relays blind over the power lines: the house could be switched and could report nothing. Ring, Alexa, and Google Home gave the house eyes and ears and left it paralyzed—the last-inch problem, in the trade’s term: the system can report that the door is open and cannot close it. Crestron and Lutron wired nervous systems into luxury houses at $50,000 to $250,000 an installation, and a wired house still could not pick a wet towel off the floor. Physical AI is the first era that gives the house hands: a generalist machine, dropped into an unmodified home, that acts on what the sensors report. The 2026 ledger of that promise, counted in order pages, contains exactly one entry.

1X’s NEO is the one humanoid a consumer can order. The price is $20,000 to own or $499 a month, against a $200 refundable deposit, with United States deliveries starting in 2026. Preorders opened on October 28, 2025, and 1X states that its first year of production capacity—more than 10,000 units, from a Hayward factory rated at 10,000 units a year—sold out within five days. The caveat is printed on the same record: NEO is not autonomous in 2026. Scheduled human teleoperation, which 1X calls Expert Mode, bridges the tasks the software has not mastered, under owner approval, with no-go zones the machine may not enter and face blurring for the people it sees. The order page sells a machine and a supervised service in one contract.

Tesla’s Optimus stands at the opposite entry: not for sale at any price. Early production began at Fremont in October 2026 on a line designed for roughly a million units a year, and more than 1,000 third-generation units work inside Tesla’s own factories. Deliveries outside the company are targeted around the end of 2027, industrial customers first. The $20,000 to $30,000 figure attached to Optimus in public discussion is an at-scale cost target stated by Elon Musk; it is not a price, and Tesla’s own annual report states that the company has “yet to commercialize Bots.” Figure’s current machine is Figure 03: it works in BMW pilots at Leipzig, its predecessor Figure 02 contributed to the production of more than 30,000 BMW X3s at Spartanburg, more than 350 Figure 03 units had been delivered by April 2026, and the commercial structure is robot-as-a-service at a reported rate near $25 an hour; Figure publishes no consumer price and sells no consumer machine. Boston Dynamics’ Atlas carries no published price, and its 2026 production is committed to Hyundai and Google DeepMind. Unitree’s machines are genuinely orderable today as research platforms; among humanoids with published prices, the trackers’ range runs from Unitree’s $4,900 R1 upward. The software under all of them is one stack in the reporting: Vision-Language-Action models paired with world models—Nvidia’s Cosmos and GR00T line is the named stack—split into a slow reasoning layer and a fast reflex layer, trained heavily in simulation for transfer to the physical world and on egocentric human video. Nvidia’s own physical-AI releases, Cosmos Transfer and Predict 2.5 on January 5, 2026 and the Isaac platform advances of October 21, 2026, stand on its newsroom as the stack’s dated entries.

What the Week’s Record Shows

Four entries, each closed by its own instrument. A resignation, closed by an 8-K: the founder of the industry’s largest company out in a week, on conduct, with the board’s confidence statement and its reversal four days apart in the same record. A product launch, closed by a spec sheet: the challenger’s silicon arriving two days before the vacancy, framed by the financial press against the vacancy before the vacancy existed in public. A proof, closed by a kernel: the oldest open problem in mathematics claimed twice in one day, the machine’s version checked to its axioms within hours and the human’s version committed to months of reading. And a robot, closed by an order page: exactly one, and the one that can be ordered arrives with a human being at its controls. The week’s technology record, besides Anthropic, the outages, and GTA VI, is those four instruments and what they certify.
